subject: Clarify residency, default retention windows and deletion triggers for prompts vs generated outputs
messages:
From: Asha Kapoor <asha.k@acmehealth.com>

Cc: procurement@acmehealth.com
Date: Sun, 09 Aug 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Clarify default retention & deletion triggers for prompts vs outputs

Vanessa —

Thanks for the kickoff call today. Procurement and our security team asked for a short written summary of the default data residency and retention behavior for developer requests. Two specific asks:  

1) By default, how long do you keep incoming requests (user prompts) and the model-generated outputs (responses)? Please call out streamed fragments vs final outputs if treated differently.
2) What are the technical triggers that cause deletion/expiry (e.g., TTL, session close, explicit customer erase request, legal hold)? What evidence do you provide back to customers after an erase?

We're not asking for contract exceptions yet — just the default hosted behavior for SRE/security review. If you can attach a small excerpt of the policy and any example logs/evidence formats that helps.

Best,
Asha Kapoor
Head of Procurement, Acme Health
asha.k@acmehealth.com

Subject: Re: Clarify default retention & deletion triggers for prompts vs outputs

Asha —

Thanks for the clear list. Summary below is the default hosted behavior (no dedicated/private contract changes). Short answer first, then specifics and evidence format.

Short answer (default hosted):
- Requests (prompts & request metadata): retained for 45 days by default.  
- Generated outputs (finalized completions or messages): retained for 45 days by default.
- Streamed fragments (partial token buffers): ephemeral — kept only in memory and transient disk buffers for up to 24 hours for recovery/forwarding; fragments are not indexed into long-term telemetry by default.
- Derivatives (embeddings, cached artifacts, KV cache dumps created by the platform for performance): may be persisted longer if the customer enables caching; default persistent retention is 90 days unless configured otherwise.

Technical deletion/expiry triggers (default hosted):
- TTL expiry: records are marked for purge automatically once they reach the configured window (45d for requests/outputs). Purge jobs run in scheduled batches and remove records from the active store.
- Explicit customer-initiated erase: customers can call our erase API or request erasure via Console; this triggers an expunge workflow that removes data from indices and triggers asynchronous purges in backups within the standard retention pipeline.
- Session close: closing a session does not immediately delete records; it only marks the session inactive. Deletion still follows TTL/erase requests.
- Legal/hold: placing a legal hold suspends purge jobs for the affected records until the hold is released. Holds are additive and require an internal legal/ops ticket to lift.

Evidence we provide after erase:
- Immediate confirmation: a job ID and timestamp acknowledging the erase request.
- Post-erasure report (available via Console and API): lists the record identifiers removed, the erase-job run id, and the completion timestamp. For hosted customers we provide a signed JSON manifest describing the top-level keys removed (example attached).
- For backup persistence: backups are rotated and retained per our backup SLA; for hosted defaults we attempt to remove erased customer records from backups within one backup cycle (up to 30 days) and include that status in the manifest.

Attachments included: redwood_retention_excerpt_v1.pdf — short policy excerpt + example erase-manifest JSON.

Notes / caveats:
- Dedicated and Private deployments can change these defaults (e.g., stricter residency, shorter TTLs) by configuration or contract.
- Streaming customers that explicitly enable long-term transcript storage should expect different retention windows.

I'll loop in Kim from Legal for the evidence wording. If Acme wants an SLA exception (shorter purge windows or guaranteed backup purging), we can scope costs and timelines.

Cheers,
Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Account Engagement
Redwood Inference

Vanessa — thanks for the summary; clear and helpful. A few legal/security clarifications for the Acme manifest and evidence so the procurement thread has what they need to sign off:  

1) Manifest format: please confirm we provide both the erase-job ID and the list of internal record UUIDs removed (we should avoid sending full user content in the manifest; instead include hashed identifiers and a checksum). The customer asked for ‘proof of deletion’ language and we should be explicit about hashes vs plaintext.

2) Backup purge SLA language: we should state the default target window (we can offer an explicit 30-day best-effort for hosted) but call out that guaranteed backup purge requires an enterprise exception. Note the customer will likely push for "guaranteed backup expunge within X days"; we should price accordingly.

3) Stream fragments: confirm that our telemetry pipeline does not promote streamed fragments to archives by default — suggest we add a short sentence in the PDF making that explicit.

Vanessa — happy to send a one-page legal-friendly paragraph you can forward into procurement. If Acme needs signed attestations we will need a redline and SOC/controls review.

Kimberly Park
Head of Legal Ops, Redwood Inference
